deep.reconstruction:
The page has drawings only; there is no text by Grothendieck. It belongs to the 1983-84 file on 'systèmes de pseudo-droites', i.e. arrangements of pseudolines in the real projective plane, drawn locally in an affine chart.

What the drawings show:
- In every figure the red strands are fixed pseudolines. They appear either as a horizontal red line crossed by red 'verticals', or as pairs of red lines crossing in an X; each X marks a vertex of the arrangement.
- The green strand is a further pseudoline (an arrow marks its orientation) that is being deformed.
- Thick black segments mark the portion of the green curve that is about to move. Grey pencil curves, numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 with arrows, show the successive positions of the green curve.

The two kinds of figure:
1. Upper-left, middle-left and middle-right figures. The green line crosses the red horizontal line. That crossing point is pushed successively past the vertical red lines (steps 1, 2, 3). At each step a triangle bounded by green, red-horizontal and one red-vertical is swept through. This is the elementary 'triangle flip' (mutation, Reidemeister-III-type move) of a pseudoline arrangement. The return arrows labelled 2 on the grey curves suggest the reverse move, or an alternative order of moves.
2. Remaining figures (upper-right, centre, bottom). The green line passes near the vertices of several X's. It is deformed by 'dips' or 'bumps', pushed below or above a vertex. That moves the green line across the vertex, again a triangle flip on the triangle formed by the green line and the two branches of the X.
   - In the bottom-centre figure, four such vertices are crossed in order 1-4, alternating downward and upward.
   - The lone figure at bottom left shows two horizontal lines and an X with a circular arrow. It seems to indicate a turning (rotation) of the local configuration.
- Several figures are crossed out in red, presumably abandoned or incorrect sequences.
- The isolated red horizontal line at the top is a separate stroke.

What problem it serves. Grothendieck seems to be studying how a pseudoline can be moved through an arrangement by elementary vertex-crossings, and in what order. This is the combinatorics of the flip graph: Ringel's theorem that any two simple arrangements are connected by triangle flips, and sweeping a line through an arrangement.

The next page is consistent with this reading. It counts crossings or moves with parameters n, ν, ν' and sign sequences ±1 and ε, where ε depends on whether a 'special form' is of 'sommital' type. So the moves drawn here appear to be the case analysis behind that count.

The paper is the back of a 1982 IBM/JES2 job log, printed upside down. It has no mathematical content.
errors: No textual claims to check. Some sequences are crossed out by Grothendieck himself, apparently as abandoned attempts; nothing else identifiable as an error.

ideas.what: Moving a pseudoline across a vertex of the arrangement (sweeping the triangle formed by three pseudolines)
ideas.modern_name: triangle flip / mutation of pseudoline arrangements (Reidemeister III move)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ringel 1956; later Goodman–Pollack, Felsner, Björner et al. (oriented matroids)

ideas.what: Successive deformation of one pseudoline through a sequence of vertices or crossing lines (numbered steps 1-4)
ideas.modern_name: topological sweep / flip sequences, connectivity of the flip graph

deep.surprise_reason: These are working sketches of standard elementary moves on pseudoline arrangements. Their interest is only as evidence of Grothendieck's hands-on combinatorial approach; nothing on this page goes beyond known material.
transcription_corrections: Small labels on the diagrams also include a symbol near the left of the upper-left green line, reading like '4' or '$' (unclear).
There is a label '1' below the middle-right figure.
There is an isolated red horizontal stroke at the top centre.
The bottom-left figure has two horizontal lines (light green and dark green) through a red X, with circular arrows.
